newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Rice, jeeps and radios free Sudan hostages.
newsitem.headline: Rice, jeeps and radios free Sudan hostages.

text.p: An offer of five tonnes of rice, four jeeps and Western radios helped to secure the release of three staff members of the International Committee of the Red Cross after 38 days of captivity in rebel hands in south Sudan.

Australian nurse Maree Worthington, American pilot John Early and Kenyan pilot Mohsin Raza flew out of the Sudanese bush to Geneva on board a U.S. military plane on Monday to a welcome with flowers and cameras.
"I think I'll get a safer job in a nuclear reactor or something," Worthington, 26, dressed in red jeans and a sweatshirt, told reporters at the Geneva airport.

The three fell into the hands of militia led by Commander Kerubino Kwanyin Kol on November 1 when their plane landed at Wunrok in southern Sudan to take home five Sudanese soldier patients discharged from a Red Cross hospital in northern Kenya.
The rebels, a breakaway group of the rebel Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), accused the ICRC of providing assistance to the mainstream SPLA.

They first demanded $100 million to free their hostages and then came down to $2.5 million. They were finally tempted into a deal with promises of supplies from ICRC stocks and a health survey in their disease-ridden camp.

It took an intervention on the ground by U.S. Congressman Bill Richardson, Democrat of New Mexico, to secure a deal after tough negotiations under a tree in the middle of the African bush with rebel leader Kerubino and his eight gun-toting commanders, each with different views.

"It was a very surreal atmosphere. The rebels were very tough negotiators," said Richardson, a personal friend of U.S. President Bill Clinton who has an unusual track record of springing American hostages.

Only last week, Richardson negotiated the release of an American held in North Korea on spying charges, the second U.S. citizen he has recovered there. He sprang two U.S. contract workers from Iraq in July 1995, and brought three political prisoners out of Cuba to the United States in February 1996.
"This was one of my toughest," he told reporters.

Asked about his success secret, he said: "You have to listen, you have to show respect and understand the other side's position. The rebel commander was a very charismatic but unpredictable man. We ended up with a common bond."
After this first Africa mission, Richardson said he would be ready to go on other springing trips to the troubled continent.
The three ICRC captives lived in a mud hut, dined on goat meat and whiled away their time playing games and reading a novel sent by the ICRC on U.S. prisoners of war in Vietnam.
Pilot Early, 51, said he taught Worthington how to tell the difference between incoming and outgoing bullets when the village was attacked by rival rebels and how to play gin rummy.
Early said he was not going back to Africa. "I'm getting tired of being shot at," said the ICRC pilot, who has worked in other African hotspots in Somalia, Burundi, Rwanda and Zaire.
Early's family called in Congressman Richardson, who visited both Khartoum and the militia-held town of Gogrial.
The militia is still holding the patients from the plane and the Red Cross said it would do everything possible to ensure they can go back to their families, who live in the area.

The SPLA has been fighting for autonomy of the mainly Christian and animist south against Khartoum's Moslem government for 13 years. Most of the victims have been civilians displaced from their homes or reduced to starvation.
